population: Generally healthy, nonpregnant adults, with no medication use, kidney disease, or other supplement/caffeine intake assumed. Reference options; individual suitability is not screened.
method: Official evidence assessments and systematic reviews of randomized trials. A physiological role is not proof of a benefit from extra supplementation. Conditional and insufficient-evidence compounds are excluded from automatic daily selection.

supplements.name: Creatine

benefits.claim: Supports repeated high-intensity efforts and strength-training adaptation over weeks.
Some reviews show a memory signal, but population, dose and response vary. Does not independently trigger a recommendation.

effectiveDose.range: 3–5 g/day without requiring a loading phase
effectiveDose.duration: Several weeks; not an acute effect.

supplements.selection: Strength priority at least 2 selects one fixed 3 g daily reference. This priority threshold is a product preference rule, not a clinical cutoff.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Exercise and athletic performance

supplements.name: Caffeine
supplements.form: Measured caffeine amount; never bulk pure powder

benefits.claim: Improves alertness acutely; does not treat chronic fatigue or replace sleep.

effectiveDose.range: 75 mg per quantified portion supports attention/alertness claims
effectiveDose.duration: One early-day portion, at least 8 hours before bedtime; not a requirement for daily use.

supplements.selection: One 75 mg portion when Focus or Energy is at least 2 and outweighs Sleep and Calm. Sleep or Calm at 4–5 always vetoes caffeine. Product conflict rules are conservative preferences, not a validated clinical score.

supplements.name: L-theanine

benefits.claim: A single 200 mg dose improved choice reaction time in a 2026 meta-analysis; a laboratory attention effect does not establish sustained daily benefit.

effectiveDose.range: 200 mg once, 30–60 minutes before cognitive testing
effectiveDose.duration: Short-term testing; no automatic daily dose.

supplements.selection: Excluded from the daily reference plan: long-term daily benefit and individualized suitability remain unverified. Not scored for Calm or Sleep.
limitations: One coauthor of the 2026 review founded a supplement company.
Stress estimates were influenced by high-bias studies; anxiety effects were inconsistent.

sources.title: Mátyus et al. 2025, healthy-adult cognitive trials

supplements.name: Magnesium

benefits.claim: Sleep studies are small or conflicting; a physiological role in nerves and muscles is not evidence that extra magnesium benefits adequately nourished adults.

supplements.selection: No automatic recommendation without an assessed dietary shortfall or clinical indication.

sources.title: NCCIH: Sleep disorders and complementary approaches

supplements.name: Vitamin D

benefits.claim: Supports normal bone and muscle function; correcting a deficiency differs from boosting a sufficient healthy adult.

effectiveDose.range: Adult RDA 600 IU ages 19–70, 800 IU over 70; total intake, not an automatic supplement prescription.

supplements.selection: Excluded pending intake or deficiency assessment.

supplements.name: Omega-3

benefits.claim: Routine fish-oil supplementation has not established general cognitive enhancement.

supplements.selection: Excluded without a specific indication. High-dose triglyceride treatment is clinician directed.

supplements.name: Melatonin

benefits.claim: May help circadian timing problems such as jet lag. Evidence does not support a blanket chronic-insomnia recommendation.

supplements.selection: Excluded without a timing indication. Long-term safety is not established.
